name: Bosnian
family: Indo-European, Balto-Slavic, Slavic, South Slavic (western group, Serbo-Croatian)
variety: Standard Bosnian (Neo-Štokavian Ijekavian norm as used in Sarajevo). Speakers in Bosnia and Herzegovina generally keep the four pitch accents and much of the post-accentual length.
sources: Jahić, Dževad; Halilović, Senahid & Palić, Ismail (2000). Gramatika bosanskoga jezika. Zenica: Dom štampe.
Riđanović, Midhat (2012). Bosnian for Foreigners: With a Comprehensive Grammar. Sarajevo: Rabic.
Lehiste, Ilse & Ivić, Pavle (1986). Word and Sentence Prosody in Serbocroatian. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
Inkelas, Sharon & Zec, Draga (1988). Serbo-Croatian pitch accent: the interaction of tone, stress, and intonation. Language 64, 227-248.
Godjevac, Svetlana (2005). Transcribing Serbo-Croatian intonation. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology: The Phonology of Intonation and Phrasing. Oxford University Press.
Browne, Wayles (1993). Serbo-Croat. In B. Comrie & G. G. Corbett (eds.), The Slavonic Languages. London: Routledge.
Landau, Ernestina; Lončarić, Mijo; Horga, Damir & Škarić, Ivo (1999). Croatian. In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, 66-69. Cambridge University Press. (same segment inventory)
contrasts: four word accents: short falling (kȕća), long falling (mȃjka), short rising (vòda), long rising (rúka)
vowel length under the accent and in syllables after the accent
postalveolar /t͡ʃ d͡ʒ/ (č, dž) versus alveolo-palatal /t͡ɕ d͡ʑ/ (ć, đ); the norm keeps them apart, many speakers in Bosnia merge them
/x/ is a stable phoneme and is kept in more words than in the Serbian and Croatian norms (lahko, mehko, kahva)
syllabic /r̩/, short or long, as a syllable nucleus that can carry the accent (krv, prst)
voiced versus voiceless obstruents, kept word-finally
allophony: the long reflex of jat, written ije, is pronounced in one syllable as a diphthong or long [jeː] (mlijeko, lijep); the short reflex je is [je]
no final devoicing; obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member, mostly shown in the spelling, also between a proclitic and its host (od kuće [ot kut͡ɕe])
/ʋ/ is a weak labiodental approximant and neither causes nor undergoes voicing assimilation
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars; /m/ is [ɱ] before /f ʋ/
/t d/ are dental; /r/ is an alveolar trill or tap
vowels keep their quality in unstressed syllables in the standard; colloquial Sarajevo speech shortens and drops unstressed short vowels, especially /i/
syllable_structure: (C)(C)(C)V(C)(C), with syllabic r as a possible nucleus
phonotactics: falling accents occur only on the first syllable of a word, rising accents on any syllable except the last; monosyllables have only falling accents
long vowels occur in the accented syllable and after it, never before it
proclitics can take over the accent of a word with a falling accent (u grad: ȕ grād)

stress.type: free (lexical) pitch accent, restricted by position
stress.rule: The accented syllable is lexical; it is never the last syllable of a polysyllabic word, and falling accents are limited to the first syllable. Ordinary spelling does not mark accent or length.
stress.cues: pitch pattern over the accented and the following syllable, duration, and intensity; vowel quality does not change

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in the standard; colloquial speech in Bosnia reduces unstressed short vowels
rhythm.notes: The class label is an impression from the descriptive literature.

length.notes: Long accented vowels are about one and a half times as long as short accented ones (Lehiste & Ivić 1986, for Serbo-Croatian in general); post-accentual long vowels are shorter than accented long vowels.

intonation.declarative: each accented word carries its lexical accent shape; successive peaks are downstepped and the phrase ends low
intonation.yes_no_question: questions with li, je li or da li end low like statements, with the verb or the focus high; questions marked by intonation alone have a low accented syllable on the focused word and a high peak on the next syllable whatever the lexical accent
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: falling accents: peak at the start of the accented syllable, low afterwards; rising accents: low to rising pitch on the accented syllable with the peak on the following syllable
intonation.notes: Described from the general Serbo-Croatian literature; I know of no separate instrumental study of Bosnian intonation that I can cite with confidence.

inventory.name: short falling (kratkosilazni), marked ȁ
inventory.description: short accented vowel with the pitch peak at its beginning and a fall; the following syllable is low. Only on first syllables and monosyllables

inventory.name: long falling (dugosilazni), marked ȃ
inventory.description: long accented vowel with an early peak and a fall through the vowel; the following syllable is low. Only on first syllables and monosyllables

inventory.name: short rising (kratkouzlazni), marked à
inventory.description: short accented vowel with level or slightly rising pitch; the following syllable is as high or higher and carries the fall. Never on the last syllable

inventory.name: long rising (dugouzlazni), marked á
inventory.description: long accented vowel with pitch rising through the vowel; the following syllable starts high and then falls. Never on the last syllable

sandhi: a proclitic before a word with a falling accent can take over the accent (u grad: ȕ grād; ne znam: nè znām); this transfer is especially regular in Bosnian usage
in intonation questions the lexical accent shapes are replaced by one low-high pattern on the focused word
tone.neutral_tone: syllables before the accent are mid; syllables after a falling accent are low; the first syllable after a rising accent is high and the rest are low
tone.notes: Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the descriptions in Lehiste & Ivić (1986) and Inkelas & Zec (1988), not measured values.

problems: There is no Bosnian pronunciation of its own: the voice uses the Croatian phoneme table (phonemes hr) and the shared rule file; the conditional entries ?3 and ?4 change only the names of some symbols and numbers.
No pitch accent: the four accents are not distinguished and accent marks in the text are ignored, except that acute-marked vowels are read as long.
No vowel length apart from a handful of words.
Stress is always on the first syllable, which is wrong for words with a rising accent on a later syllable (ljepòta, telèvīzija).
Syllabic r between consonants is a plain consonant and not a syllable nucleus: krv, prst, trg, smrt have no stressed syllable, and prvi, crkva, brzo are stressed on the last vowel.
Unstressed /a i u/ are replaced by reduced qualities (& [æ]-like, [ɪ], [ʊ]); the standard has no vowel reduction.
The long jat reflex ije is read as two syllables [i.je] (mlijeko, lijep).
h is [x] at the start of a word and [h] elsewhere; Bosnian keeps a velar fricative in all positions.
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
good: č and ć, dž and đ are kept apart
regressive voicing assimilation, also between words (od kuće [ot])
lj and nj as single palatals [ʎ ɲ]
Cyrillic input is converted to Latin

notes: Segment inventory and accent system are those of the common Neo-Štokavian standard; see also hr and sr. No formant, VOT or rhythm-metric values are given because I cannot quote published figures with confidence.
